_Why must a physical AI systems engineer master mechanical inertia, winding thermal limits, and power distribution rail droop before writing a single line of motor control policy?_

A mobile manipulator can recognize an obstacle correctly and still strike it if its body cannot stop within the remaining distance. The same machine can hold a payload without moving while its motor windings overheat, or lose its controller when a sudden demand for current pulls the supply voltage too low. These failures arise from limits that prediction accuracy alone cannot reveal. Physical AI engineering requires connecting a proposed action to the motion, heat, and electrical demand it creates, then establishing which limit the assembled machine reaches first. Measurements must also establish the conditions under which those limits hold, because a change in payload, floor surface, cooling, or battery state changes what the machine can deliver. The body's limits therefore govern what the permission path may admit before a command crosses the causal boundary and produces irreversible physical work.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate observation freshness limits from measurement age and the machine's allowable motion
- Calculate stopping distance and the admissible speed ceiling from pre-brake delay, credible deceleration, and clearance overheads
- Evaluate actuator and transmission choices against response limits, reflected inertia, and mechanical impedance
- Estimate sustainable motor duty cycles from heat generation, cooling, and operating conditions
- Budget electrical supply margins for simultaneous actuation, computation, and regenerative braking
- Specify the elements of a limit record that states a measured limit's conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and evidence category
- Evaluate maneuver-specific binding budgets from qualified evidence and justify holding up the permission supply through covered faults

:::

## The Five Physical Budgets {#sec-body-five-budgets}

Every action a learned model proposes ultimately manifests as electrical current flowing through a motor winding, and from that instant physics governs execution. Machine learning practice rarely contends with this transition. Policies trained in simulation typically interact with idealized plants where commanded torque appears instantaneously, heat never accumulates in windings, and direct current (DC) bus voltages never sag under load. A physical machine honors none of these simplifications. The **physical body**\index{Physical body!definition} is the coupled assembly of actuators, mechanical transmissions, structural linkages, power electronics, and sensors that translates digital commands into mechanical motion. Its physical dynamics bound what even a mathematically optimal policy can achieve. An emergency brake command requires finite time to develop mechanical retarding force and clearance distance to dissipate kinetic energy. Similarly, commanding a manipulator to hold a heavy payload motionless draws continuous phase current, dissipating resistive heat into the stator even though the joint does zero mechanical work.

The proposal boundary in @sec-boundary-machine-model assigns the permission path responsibility for admitting action, and the body provides the concrete physical envelopes that make that gating decision meaningful. Before committing a command to hardware registers, the permission path must evaluate five fundamental physical budgets: it must confirm that the sensor observation remains fresh, that the moving machine can stop within available clearance, that the actuator can deliver the required torque trajectory, that the winding can tolerate the resulting thermal rise, and that the electrical bus can support the transient current demand. These mechanisms form a direct causal chain: sensor and pipeline latencies consume allowable stopping distance; arresting momentum demands delivered actuator torque; generating that torque dissipates heat in motor coils and pulls current from a shared power rail. For any given maneuver, the governing systems question is which of these physical budgets binds first, under what operational stress, and on what empirical evidence.

1. **Measurement freshness** ($\ObservationAge$)\index{Measurement freshness!definition}: The observation must remain valid until the mechanical plant responds. Latency accumulated across sensor exposure, data transport, neural inference, and low-level drive dispatch consumes allowable tracking margins as the physical world continues to move.
2. **Kinetic momentum** ($\KineticEnergy, \LinearMomentum$)\index{Kinetic momentum!definition}: A moving machine carries kinetic energy ($\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \BodySpeed^2$) and linear or angular momentum ($\LinearMomentum = \Mass \BodySpeed$). Bringing the plant to rest demands applying retarding force over finite distance and time; safe operating velocity must therefore preserve a stopping envelope well within available physical clearance.
3. **Actuator bandwidth and reflected inertia** ($\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$)\index{Actuator bandwidth!definition}\index{Reflected inertia|see{Reflected rotor inertia}}: Winding inductance and supply voltage limit the rate at which torque can change. A gearhead with reduction ratio $\GearReductionRatio$ multiplies delivered torque by $\GearReductionRatio$, but it also scales the motor rotor's inertia $\RotorInertia$ by $\GearReductionRatio^2$ as seen at the joint output (@sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia), fundamentally constraining instantaneous acceleration.
4. **Thermal capacity** ($\EstimatedWindingTemperature$)\index{Thermal capacity!definition}: Resistive losses ($\WindingLossPower = \TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \EffectiveLossResistance$, with $\EffectiveLossResistance$ the winding's effective loss resistance) deposit thermal energy directly into the stator windings and inverter switching stages. Heat dissipation limits sustained continuous torque, while the thermal mass of the coils constrains the magnitude, duration, and repetition rate of transient torque bursts.
5. **Electrical power integrity** ($\DcRailVoltage$)\index{Electrical power integrity!definition}: Onboard compute clusters and motor inverters draw from a shared DC power rail. Peak motor accelerations must not drag the bus voltage below digital logic thresholds, while regenerative braking must provide an electrical sink so returned kinetic energy does not overvoltage the bus.

Under the **simultaneous admission invariant**\index{Simultaneous admission invariant!definition}, motion permission requires a non-negative margin in every budget before the permission path commits torque to hardware registers. Each margin must be checked in its own units; time, distance, torque, temperature, and voltage are separate constraints, not interchangeable quantities:
$$\begin{aligned}
\ObservationAge &\le \TelemetryFreshnessBound, \\
\StoppingDistance &\le \ClearDistance, \\
|\CommandedJointTorque| &\le \OutputTorqueCeiling, \\
\EstimatedWindingTemperature &\le \WindingTemperatureLimit, \\
\MinimumRailVoltage &\ge \ConverterLockoutVoltage.
\end{aligned}$$
Here $\CommandedJointTorque$ is requested torque and $\OutputTorqueCeiling$ is the maximum deliverable output torque under current electrical and thermal conditions. The estimated winding temperature $\EstimatedWindingTemperature$ must remain below its limit, while the lowest rail voltage $\MinimumRailVoltage$ must remain above the undervoltage-lockout threshold $\ConverterLockoutVoltage$ at which the supply regulator shuts down. The fifth line checks only undervoltage. Permission must also require regenerative braking to stay below the qualified upper operating-voltage limit of the supplied components, with an available absorption or dissipation path. Two lines state their budgets in derived form. The kinetic budget appears as the stopping distance it demands, $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$, and the actuator line checks only torque magnitude, because the slew-rate limit that winding inductance and reflected inertia impose enters the stopping line instead, through the brake-onset term of the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$. All five inequalities must hold simultaneously. A surplus in four budgets cannot compensate for a deficit in the fifth: a fresh observation cannot prevent a stop from overrunning if kinetic energy exceeds available clearance, and abundant battery energy cannot prevent an actuator from burning out if thermal dissipation limits are violated.

::: {.callout-perspective title="Why physical limits bound physical AI architecture"}
The permission path requires concrete bounds on physical behavior, not abstract software promises. Accepting a torque command does not guarantee that the inverter can deliver the requested current against the back electromotive force (back-EMF) the spinning motor induces in its own windings, nor does cutting motor power guarantee that friction will arrest the plant before it breaches a clearance zone. The five physical budgets bridge this gap, tying software proposals to verifiable, empirical responses under declared operating conditions.
:::

```{python}
#| label: body-machine-momentum-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S MOMENTUM (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the running-machine sentence in @sec-body-five-budgets.
# │ Goal:    Give the warehouse mobile manipulator's kinetic energy at its
# │          drive limit with the tote rack loaded.
# │ Show:    368 kg (upper bound) at 1.5 m/s carries 414 J.
# │ How:     calc_kinetic_energy on RM.loaded_mass and RM.base.max_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_mass, fmt_velocity, fmt_energy, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineMomentum:
    """Kinetic energy of the loaded running machine at its drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m_loaded = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound, full tote rack)
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    e_k = calc_kinetic_energy(m_loaded, v_drive).to(joule)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_loaded.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected loaded mass: {m_loaded}")
    check(abs(e_k.magnitude - 414.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected kinetic energy: {e_k}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    m_loaded_str = fmt_mass(m_loaded, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    e_k_str = fmt_energy(e_k, unit=joule, precision=0)
```

The warehouse mobile manipulator that this book follows draws on all five. Loaded to at most `{python} MachineMomentum.m_loaded_str` and moving at its `{python} MachineMomentum.v_drive_str` drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), it carries `{python} MachineMomentum.e_k_str` of kinetic energy through aisles it shares with people.

Each budget establishes an empirical operating boundary on the assembled machine under declared thermal and electrical stress, and each ends the chapter as a limit record, the six-element record that @sec-boundary-book-architecture sketched from the stopping notebook: a value, the conditions under which it holds, its uncertainty, the margin defended, a runtime detector, and the provenance of its evidence. The first budget is the age of the measurement on which every command rests, which runs from physical transduction, well before any software process receives the raw sensor data.

## Measurement Freshness {#sec-body-measurement-freshness}

```{python}
#| label: body-latency-profile-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PICK STATION'S FRESHNESS DEADLINE AND AGE PROFILE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the opening and freshness-deadline paragraphs, the definition,
# │          \ref{nbk-body-freshness-deadline}, @tbl-02-latency-breakdown,
# │          the freshness item of \ref{chk-body-bus-droop-regen}, and the
# │          first problem of @sec-body-problems. (2026-09-29: the waterfall
# │          figure was cut; @tbl-04-event-ledger carries the running
# │          machine's ledger. 2026-09-30: re-anchored from an upstream parcel
# │          sorter to the running machine's pick-station conveyor.)
# │ Goal:    Hold the conveyor's deadline and the illustrative stage profile in
# │          one place so the prose, the table, the notebook, the checkpoint,
# │          and the problem cannot disagree.
# │ Show:    0.20 m/s conveyor, 15 mm grasp tolerance less 3 mm initial error
# │          = 12 mm, so a 60 ms deadline; stage P50 sum 35.0 ms, P99 sum
# │          50.0 ms, max sum 80.7 ms; system P99 46.2 ms and P99.9 68.4 ms;
# │          7 mm of mug travel at the median (5 mm inside the tolerance) and
# │          13.7 mm at P99.9 (1.7 mm past it).
# │ How:     Delta t_fresh = (r_tol - e_0) / v_conv from AISLE; stage sums;
# │          travel = v_conv * age. Every stage value is illustrative: a
# │          measured profile of the integrated machine replaces it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_frequency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class GraspLatencyProfile:
    """Freshness deadline for the conveyor mug and an illustrative capture-to-onset profile."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_conv = AISLE.v_conveyor  # category: illustrative (pick-station conveyor speed)
    r_tol = AISLE.grasp_tolerance  # category: chosen (grasp tolerance)
    e_0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error  # category: illustrative (initial estimate error)
    # (name, P50, P99, max) in ms; category: illustrative (not a measured profile)
    stages = [
        ("1–2. Exposure and readout", 11.2, 16.6, 16.7),
        ("3–4. Transport and DMA", 1.4, 3.2, 6.8),
        ("5. Backbone and policy", 18.5, 24.1, 38.4),
        ("6. Scheduling and IPC", 0.6, 2.1, 12.3),
        ("7. Fieldbus", 1.0, 1.0, 2.0),
        ("8. Current rise", 2.3, 3.0, 4.5),
    ]
    sys_p99 = 46.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (system-level profile)
    sys_p999 = 68.4 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (system-level tail)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    e_max = (r_tol - e_0).to(millimeter)  # the tolerance the mug's motion may spend
    t_fresh = (e_max / v_conv).to(millisecond)
    t_backbone = stages[2][1] * millisecond
    sum_p50 = sum(s[1] for s in stages) * millisecond
    sum_p99 = sum(s[2] for s in stages) * millisecond
    sum_max = sum(s[3] for s in stages) * millisecond
    travel_p50 = (v_conv * sum_p50).to(millimeter)
    travel_p999 = (v_conv * sys_p999).to(millimeter)
    margin_p50 = (e_max - travel_p50).to(millimeter)
    excess_p999 = (travel_p999 - e_max).to(millimeter)
    t_rest_p50 = sum_p50 - t_backbone  # every stage but the backbone
    f_backbone = (1 / t_backbone).to(ureg.hertz)  # the loop rate a backbone benchmark suggests

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_conv.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.20) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected conveyor speed: {v_conv}")
    check(abs(r_tol.to(millimeter).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected grasp tolerance: {r_tol}")
    check(abs(e_0.to(millimeter).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected initial error: {e_0}")
    check(abs(t_fresh.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Conveyor freshness deadline must be 60 ms: {t_fresh}")
    check(abs(sum_p50.magnitude - 35.0) < 1e-9, f"P50 stage sum drifted: {sum_p50}")
    check(abs(sum_p99.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"P99 stage sum drifted: {sum_p99}")
    check(abs(sum_max.magnitude - 80.7) < 1e-9, f"Max stage sum drifted: {sum_max}")
    check(sys_p99 < sum_p99, "The system P99 must differ from (here, sit below) the stage-P99 sum.")
    check(
        abs(travel_p50.magnitude - 7.0) < 1e-9 and abs(margin_p50.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9,
        "The notebook states 7 mm of median travel, 5 mm inside the tolerance.",
    )
    check(
        abs(travel_p999.magnitude - 13.68) < 1e-9 and abs(excess_p999.magnitude - 1.68) < 1e-9,
        f"Tail travel drifted: {travel_p999}",
    )
    check(abs(t_rest_p50.magnitude - 16.5) < 1e-9, f"Non-backbone median share drifted: {t_rest_p50}")
    check(
        t_backbone < sum_p50 < sys_p99 < t_fresh < sys_p999,
        "The backbone, the median chain, and the P99 fit the deadline; the P99.9 tail must not.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_conv_str = fmt_velocity(v_conv, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(r_tol, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e_0_str = fmt_length(e_0, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_fresh_str = fmt_latency(t_fresh, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sum_p50_str = fmt_latency(sum_p50, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sum_p99_str = fmt_latency(sum_p99, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sys_p99_str = fmt_latency(sys_p99, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sys_p999_str = fmt_latency(sys_p999, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(t_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_rest_p50_str = fmt_latency(t_rest_p50, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_p50_mm_str = fmt_length(travel_p50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    margin_p50_mm_str = fmt_length(margin_p50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    travel_p999_mm_str = fmt_length(travel_p999, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    excess_p999_mm_str = fmt_length(excess_p999, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    f_backbone_str = fmt_frequency(f_backbone, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=1)
    # @tbl-02-latency-breakdown cells: stage k (1-6) at P50, P99, and max, in ms;
    # integer-like values print without a dead decimal (house precision guard).
    s1_p50_str, s1_p99_str, s1_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[0][1:])
    s2_p50_str, s2_p99_str, s2_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[1][1:])
    s3_p50_str, s3_p99_str, s3_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[2][1:])
    s4_p50_str, s4_p99_str, s4_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[3][1:])
    s5_p50_str, s5_p99_str, s5_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[4][1:])
    s6_p50_str, s6_p99_str, s6_max_str = (fmt(x, precision=0 if round(float(x), 6).is_integer() else 1) for x in stages[5][1:])
    sum_p50_num_str = fmt(sum_p50.magnitude, precision=0 if round(float(sum_p50.magnitude), 6).is_integer() else 1)
    sum_p99_num_str = fmt(sum_p99.magnitude, precision=0 if round(float(sum_p99.magnitude), 6).is_integer() else 1)
    sum_max_num_str = fmt(sum_max.magnitude, precision=0 if round(float(sum_max.magnitude), 6).is_integer() else 1)
    sys_p99_num_str = fmt(sys_p99.magnitude, precision=0 if round(float(sys_p99.magnitude), 6).is_integer() else 1)
```

Software benchmarks in machine learning frequently report latency as isolated accelerator execution time, for example `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str` for the vision backbone of the arm's wrist-camera grasp path on an edge neural processing unit (NPU), a different pipeline from the navigation backbone that the stopping budget of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline charges. This narrow focus fosters the illusion of an agile `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.f_backbone_str` control loop. In physical AI systems, however, that compute kernel represents only one intermediate segment in an end-to-end silicon-to-plant dataflow pipeline. A sensor measurement begins decaying the moment physical transduction occurs; what governs physical performance is its total age when torque actually appears at the actuator joint. That physical age spans the entire interval from the moment photons strike a photodiode array, magnetic flux sweeps past a Hall sensor, or strain deflects a piezoresistor to the moment motor inverter switches build stator magnetic flux that alters link acceleration. If a perception policy evaluates an obstacle bounding box in `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str`, while exposure integration, sensor readout, Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) transport, kernel scheduling, fieldbus dispatch, and motor current rise consume an additional `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_rest_p50_str` at the median, the true physical age of the observation when the joint accelerates is `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str`, and the distribution tail extends farther still.

Throughout that capture-to-onset window, the physical environment continues to evolve unobserved. In distributed data systems, read-after-write consistency windows govern whether a client observes stale or linearized state. In physical AI, the physical plant acts as an autonomous, unpausable concurrent writer: spatial position $\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant)$ evolves along continuous trajectories at velocity $\Velocity(\TimeInstant)$. An observation age $\ObservationAge$ converts directly into unobserved physical displacement $\FiniteChange \CartesianPosition \approx \int_0^{\ObservationAge} \Velocity(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant$. High-speed machines inevitably act on historical state.

The rate of world-state change dictates how long a measurement remains valid before acting on it introduces intolerable error. Let $\PositionErrorCeiling$ denote the maximum acceptable error in a tracked state, such as a joint angle or the position of a part on a conveyor, and let $\SpeedBound$ denote the fastest credible velocity at which that state can evolve. The freshness deadline $\TelemetryFreshnessBound$ is the upper bound on measurement age before a control action based on that measurement becomes invalid, defined by the inequality
$$\TelemetryFreshnessBound \le \frac{\PositionErrorCeiling}{\SpeedBound}$$ {#eq-body-freshness-deadline}

::: {#dfn-body-freshness-deadline .callout-definition title="Freshness deadline"}

***Freshness deadline***\index{Freshness deadline!definition} ($\TelemetryFreshnessBound$) is the largest age, counted from the capture of a measurement to the onset of the actuator's response, that the measurement of a moving target may reach before the target's motion alone spends the allowable position error $\PositionErrorCeiling$ (@eq-body-freshness-deadline).

1.  **Significance**: It converts a spatial tolerance into a time budget that every stage from exposure to torque onset must share. A `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_max_str` tolerance on a target moving at `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str` leaves `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` for sensing, inference, transport, and current rise together.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike an inference-latency budget, which times one stage, the deadline bounds the age at onset; unlike a control-loop period, it is set by the target's speed and the tolerance rather than by the loop rate. When the machine moves toward a stationary obstacle instead, the same age becomes the first term of the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ and is paid as blind travel $\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay$ in the stopping distance.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the deadline as a property of the sensor or the model. It changes whenever the target moves faster or the tolerance shrinks, so a pipeline qualified on a slow conveyor can miss on a faster one without any change in its own timing.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The same deadline applied to a stored belief, which lapses once its region falls out of view, is developed in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.
:::

The running machine meets this bound at its pick station, where the arm grasps a mug from a moving conveyor. The belt carries the mug at speeds up to $\ConveyorSpeed =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str`, and the gripper mechanism tolerates $\PositionalTaskTolerance =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.r_tol_str` of position error. Initial handle-pose estimation already consumes $\InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_0_str` of this margin. Consequently, the mug's physical motion may spend at most $\PositionErrorCeiling = \PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_max_str`, with $\SpeedBound = \ConveyorSpeed$. Notebook \ref{nbk-body-freshness-deadline} evaluates this resulting deadline against the ages an integrated camera-to-joint pipeline delivers in practice. The deadline governs any target that moves while its observation ages. For moving workpieces, it limits motion-induced tracking drift under bounded relative velocity and valid initial observations; sensing and state-estimation noise consume separate slices of the tolerance budget, just as $\InitialTrackingError$ does here. Conversely, when the robot approaches a stationary obstacle, such as a person standing in a warehouse aisle, the target does not move; instead, the mobile base drives toward the person during the latency interval. Observation age then converts directly into unguided vehicular travel before braking begins, which @sec-body-kinetic-momentum charges against the kinetic stopping envelope.

### Transduction physics, quantization noise, and Nyquist limits {#sec-body-sensor-transduction}

Sensor selection consumes both error tolerance and time. A sensor must resolve the physical state of interest, and the analog filtering, sampling, or serial scanning required to extract that signal must fit within the freshness deadline. Four physical mechanisms illustrate this design constraint:

1. **Optical Encoders and Velocity Quantization Noise:**
   An encoder measures joint position in discrete angular increments. An $\EncoderBitCount$-bit encoder discretizes the continuous $2\pi\text{ rad}$ circle into an angular resolution of $\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle = \frac{2\pi}{2^\EncoderBitCount}$. For an 18-bit absolute optical encoder, $\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad}$ ($0.0014^\circ$); for a 12-bit magnetic encoder, $\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle \approx 1.53 \times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}$ ($0.088^\circ$). Feedback controllers estimate joint velocity from successive position samples across a discrete control cycle $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$:
   $${\EncoderVelocityEstimate{}}_{k} \approx \frac{{\EncoderAngle}_{k} - {\EncoderAngle}_{k-1}}{\FiniteChange \TimeInstant}$$
   Backward differencing acts as an effective high-pass filter, scaling high-frequency position fluctuations by $1/\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$. Under an idealized model where successive quantization errors are independent and uniformly distributed across one encoder count, each sample has variance $(\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle)^2/12$. Differencing two independent samples sums their variances to $(\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle)^2/6$, yielding a velocity-error standard deviation of $\EncoderVelocityNoise = \frac{\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle}{\sqrt{6}\,\FiniteChange \TimeInstant}$. At a $1\text{ kHz}$ servo update rate ($\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = 1\text{ ms}$), a single-count jump on a 12-bit encoder ($1.53\text{ mrad}$) registers as an abrupt velocity spike of $1.53\text{ rad/s}$ ($88^\circ/\text{s}$). If routed directly into velocity feedback loops or neural policy state inputs, these discrete impulses cause severe torque chatter and excite mechanical resonances. Downstream low-pass filters or state observers smooth this quantization noise, but filter group delay introduces phase lag, consuming milliseconds of the freshness budget.

2. **Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and Nyquist Aliasing:**
   An inertial measurement unit measures linear acceleration and angular velocity. Sampling must isolate macroscopic body dynamics from high-frequency structural vibration. Under the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem [@nyquist1928certain; @shannon1949communication], continuous signals require a sampling frequency strictly greater than twice their highest spectral component ($\SamplingRate > 2 \HighestSignalFrequency$). Mechanical sources, including gear mesh harmonics, cooling fans, and motor inverter switching, generate vibrations reaching kilohertz frequencies. Without adequate analog anti-aliasing filters before the analog-to-digital converter (ADC), structural vibrations above the Nyquist frequency fold back into baseband frequencies ($1\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$). The state estimator cannot distinguish these aliased artifacts from genuine chassis acceleration, introducing cumulative drift into dead-reckoning integrations. Raising downstream software loop rates cannot reconstruct information already corrupted at the sensor hardware interface.

3. **Tactile Sensor Arrays and Scanning Bandwidth:**
   Tactile arrays measure contact pressure across a robot gripper using discrete sensing elements called taxels. To minimize cabling across robotic wrists, hardware architectures multiplex taxels across shared row and column lines. Scanning these elements sequentially forces an entire frame to span the multiplexing period. This serial scan time adds directly to the measurement age and limits the bandwidth for detecting rapid contact events, such as the onset of localized slip. Increasing the taxel density without scaling the underlying ADC readout rate produces older tactile observations.

4. **Cameras and Rolling-Shutter Readout:**
   A rolling-shutter CMOS camera exposes and transfers pixel rows sequentially, so a single frame spans its entire readout duration. Image timestamps must therefore anchor to a defined reference, such as the exposure midpoint of a designated row, rather than the frame-arrival interrupt.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Rolling-shutter distortion on the navigation camera, and its compensation before images enter the state estimator, is developed in @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
:::

### The end-to-end sense-to-actuation latency pipeline {#sec-body-latency-pipeline}

A measurement's physical age begins at **capture**\index{Capture!event}, the moment of physical transduction, rather than when an operating system process first receives the data buffer. Three subsequent boundary events demarcate the pipeline from transduction to mechanical work: *dispatch*, when perception publishes dated perceptual evidence to the action proposer; *admission*, when the real-time permission path validates and accepts a proposal built using that evidence; and *onset*, when electrical current in the motor stator windings begins driving physical acceleration at the joint. The four events recur throughout the book, and @tbl-04-event-ledger later budgets the intervals between them for the running machine. For the freshness deadline, capture and onset form the bounding endpoints: the deadline limits the cumulative delay between them.

An illustrative camera-to-joint pipeline reveals how latency compounds across physical and digital boundaries (@tbl-02-latency-breakdown). Between capture and dispatch, the CMOS sensor integrates exposure and reads out raw scanlines over MIPI CSI-2;[^fn-mipi-frame-timestamp] direct memory access (DMA) transfers the frame into host memory, and the vision backbone executes. In this representative architecture, the policy network executes in the same inference pass as the backbone, spanning the dispatch boundary. Between dispatch and admission, inter-process communication (IPC) transmits the proposed trajectory to the safety microcontroller, a dedicated real-time processor that executes the deterministic permission path. Between admission and onset, an EtherCAT fieldbus[^fn-ethercat-cycle-time] delivers target setpoints to individual motor drives, where power-inverter gate drivers switch to ramp up stator current. Neural inference occupies one of the eight stages; under memory bus contention and scheduling delays, the peripheral system stages expand the latency tail substantially more than the neural network execution itself.

[^fn-mipi-frame-timestamp]: **MIPI CSI-2 (Camera Serial Interface 2)**\index{MIPI CSI-2!frame-start timestamp}: The Mobile Industry Processor Interface camera link carries raw frames from the image sensor to the system-on-chip and marks the start and end of each frame with short packets. Latching a hardware timestamp on the frame-start packet ties the frame to a fixed offset from its exposure rather than to the moment software first sees it, which is what lets transduction time, not arrival time, anchor the age budget.

[^fn-ethercat-cycle-time]: **EtherCAT**\index{EtherCAT!cycle determinism}: An industrial Ethernet fieldbus in which one frame passes through every drive on the segment, each node reading and writing its own slice of the frame as it passes. Frame length and node count, not contention for the wire, fix the cycle time, which is why the fieldbus row of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown has equal $\text{p50}$ and $\text{p99}$. @Sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis sizes that cycle for the running machine.

Systems engineers sometimes estimate worst-case pipeline latency by summing the 99th-percentile ($\text{p99}$) latencies of individual stages. However, the percentile of a sum does not equal the sum of the percentiles.[^fn-math-quantile-convolution] In embedded system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, shared hardware resources couple stage delays. For example, PCIe DMA bursts during camera readout contend for memory-controller bandwidth with neural accelerators, while CPU cache evictions during kernel message passing induce thread scheduling jitter. The end-to-end distribution of sense-to-torque latency must therefore be profiled empirically on the integrated hardware platform under concurrent production workloads. Furthermore, an empirical percentile remains a statistical measurement; it does not replace the formal worst-case bounds required for hard real-time safety guarantees.

[^fn-math-quantile-convolution]: **Quantile Convolution**\index{Quantile convolution!tail non-additivity}: In general, the quantile of a latency sum differs from the sum of equal-percentile stage quantiles ($\LatencyQuantileFunction(\UpstreamStageLatency + \DownstreamStageLatency) \ne \LatencyQuantileFunction(\UpstreamStageLatency) + \LatencyQuantileFunction(\DownstreamStageLatency)$). Independence alone does not make their arithmetic sum a worst-case bound. Correlation from shared buses and queues changes the end-to-end tail and must be characterized at the system boundary.

Each stage in @tbl-02-latency-breakdown carries its own tail under continuous inference load, and the two bottom rows separate the arithmetic column sums from the end-to-end age the system actually delivers.

| Pipeline Stage                     | Physical Mechanism / Contention Source                                              |                 $\text{p50}$ (ms)                  |                 $\text{p99}$ (ms)                  |                         Max (ms)                         |
|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------:|
| **1–2. Sensor Exposure & Readout** | $60\text{ Hz}$ rolling shutter exposure midpoint                                    |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s1_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s1_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s1_max_str`         |
| **3–4. Host Transport & DMA**      | PCIe DMA transfer into host memory                                                  |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s2_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s2_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s2_max_str`         |
| **5. Vision Backbone & Policy**    | Onboard accelerator inference (memory throttling tail)                              |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s3_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s3_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s3_max_str`         |
| **6. OS Scheduling & IPC**         | Kernel preemption and mailbox hand-off to safety microcontroller                    |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s4_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s4_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s4_max_str`         |
| **7. Fieldbus Transmission**       | Deterministic EtherCAT cyclic packet exchange                                       |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s5_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s5_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s5_max_str`         |
| **8. Actuator Current Rise**       | Gate driver switching and stator flux buildup                                       |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s6_p50_str`      |     `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s6_p99_str`      |        `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.s6_max_str`         |
| **Arithmetic Stage Sum**           | Sum of each column's stage values; not an end-to-end quantile                       | **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p50_num_str`** | **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p99_num_str`** |    **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_max_num_str`**    |
| **End-to-End Age**                 | System-level profile, capture to onset; max bounded within the illustrative profile | **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p50_num_str`** | **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sys_p99_num_str`** | $\le$ **`{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_max_num_str`** |

: **Illustrative sense-to-actuation latency decomposition**: Stage and system-level timings show why the arithmetic sum of stage percentiles is not the end-to-end tail. The example's $\text{p99.9}$ of `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sys_p999_str` exceeds the `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` freshness deadline of the mug on the pick-station conveyor, although its median fits. {#tbl-02-latency-breakdown tbl-colwidths="[26,38,12,12,12]"}

The `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p99_str` sum of individual stage percentiles overstates the system-level $\text{p99}$ latency of `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sys_p99_str` because pipeline stages rarely experience worst-case contention simultaneously. For the same reason, the sum of the stage maxima enters the end-to-end row only as an upper bound within the stated illustrative profile and conditions. A measured maximum needs a separately justified allowance or bound before it can support a hard real-time deadline. Coupling pushes the other way. Stages that slow down together, because they contend for the same memory controller or scheduler, fatten the end-to-end tail toward the stage sum, while stages that vary independently usually leave that sum pessimistic, as here. The end-to-end median in the table is set equal to the stage-median sum, a simplification of the illustrative profile that a measured one need not share. Notebook \ref{nbk-body-freshness-deadline} evaluates how this illustrative profile behaves against the conveyor's physical deadline.

::: {#nbk-body-freshness-deadline .callout-notebook title="The freshness deadline"}

**Problem**: The arm grasps a mug riding the pick-station conveyor, acting on camera observations of the handle. Suppose the grasp path had the illustrative age profile of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown. Does it deliver those observations within the freshness deadline, and how far does the mug move at the median and at the tail of the observation age?

**Variables**:

- Grasp tolerance $\PositionalTaskTolerance =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.r_tol_str`, of which the initial estimate spends $\InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_0_str` (illustrative)
- Conveyor speed $\SpeedBound = \ConveyorSpeed =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str` (illustrative)
- Median backbone time `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str`, median end-to-end age `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str`, and $\text{p99.9}$ age `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sys_p999_str` (illustrative profile of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown)

**Math**:

1. **Deadline**: $\PositionErrorCeiling = \PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_max_str`, so $\TelemetryFreshnessBound = \PositionErrorCeiling/\SpeedBound =$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.e_max_str` $/$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str` $=$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` (@eq-body-freshness-deadline).
2. **Backbone alone**: `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str` is less than `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str`, so the one stage a benchmark times fits with room to spare.
3. **Median chain**: `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str` $\times$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str` $=$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.travel_p50_mm_str` of mug travel, `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.margin_p50_mm_str` inside the tolerance.
4. **Tail**: `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.v_conv_str` $\times$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.sys_p999_str` $=$ `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.travel_p999_mm_str`, `{python} GraspLatencyProfile.excess_p999_mm_str` past the tolerance.

**Result**: Inference and the median chain both meet the deadline, but the stated $\text{p99.9}$ age exceeds it. The profile therefore does not establish that 99.9 percent of grasps meet the freshness deadline.

**Systems insight**: The whole path from exposure to torque onset spends the freshness deadline, not the model alone, and its tail, not its median, decides whether the grasp holds. When the machine instead drives toward a stationary obstacle, the same age enters the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ as its first term and is paid as blind travel $\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay$, the first term of the stopping distance that @sec-body-kinetic-momentum sets against the clear distance.

:::

Excessive feedback delay can also degrade closed-loop tracking or destabilize motor control loops,[^fn-delay-loop-stability] but the freshness calculation requires no frequency-domain model: at the latency tail, the mug has already moved beyond mechanical capture tolerance. System architectures must therefore preserve the observation's true physical capture timestamp. Hardware timers synchronized through **IEEE 802.1AS**\index{IEEE 802.1AS!hardware timestamping}, the generalized Precision Time Protocol (gPTP),[^fn-gptp-shared-timebase] or hardware capture strobes associated with the **MIPI CSI-2**\index{MIPI CSI-2!sensor readout interface} receiver provide a common physical timebase. The sensor's exposure and readout characteristics determine how that hardware timestamp maps to the measurement midpoint. Once latched, this capture timestamp accompanies the observation through every subsequent compute kernel.

At the admission boundary, the real-time permission path computes the observation's total elapsed age, $\ObservationAge = \CurrentWallClockTime - \TransductionInstant$, and adds the bounded remaining admission-to-onset interval for fieldbus dispatch and motor current rise. Capture and clock-synchronization uncertainty must also fit the qualified age budget. The permission path rejects the proposed trajectory update if its projected onset age exceeds the freshness deadline. Rejecting a stale trajectory replacement does not necessitate cutting motor torque immediately; an executing command may continue while its qualified physical margin remains valid. If that margin expires before fresh, valid observations arrive, the permission path triggers a qualified fallback maneuver within the remaining stopping distance [@brooks1986robust].

[^fn-delay-loop-stability]: **Transport Delay and Feedback Stability**\index{Transport delay!feedback instability}\index{Asynchronous divergence!closed-loop}: Transport delay makes a controller act on historical state. Whether delayed corrections destabilize the loop depends on the plant, controller, and total response. @Sec-appendix-control-zoh develops the phase-margin calculation; delay alone does not establish a particular oscillation or damage outcome.

[^fn-gptp-shared-timebase]: **IEEE 802.1AS (gPTP)**\index{IEEE 802.1AS!hardware timestamping}\index{IEEE 1588!Precision Time Protocol}: The generalized Precision Time Protocol of IEEE 802.1AS is a profile of the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol [@ieee15882019] for time-sensitive Ethernet networks [@ieee8021as2020]. It synchronizes clocks by exchanging packets timestamped in hardware at the network interface, which keeps the operating-system scheduler's jitter out of the measurement. The age $\ObservationAge = \CurrentWallClockTime - \TransductionInstant$ means something only when the camera, the host, and the drives read one timebase; an offset between their clocks enters the freshness budget as an error that no timestamp reveals.

::: {.callout-perspective title="The publish timestamp anti-pattern"}
A widespread architectural bug in robotics systems is timestamping sensor observations inside user-space publishers, such as a Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) node transmitting over Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware. Latching timestamps in application software discards the duration of sensor exposure, rolling-shutter integration, sensor readout, DMA transfers, and kernel queueing, and so erases stages 1 through 4 of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown (exposure, readout, transport, and DMA), along with any kernel queueing before the publisher runs, from the latency ledger. Hardware strobes must latch timestamps directly at the physical silicon interface (such as MIPI CSI-2 Start-of-Frame interrupts or Ethernet physical-layer transceiver timestamps synchronized via IEEE 802.1AS) before data enters operating-system queues.
:::

Bounding measurement age ensures that control policies act on valid observations rather than historical artifacts, but freshness alone cannot guarantee collision avoidance. Throughout that capture-to-onset interval, the body continues moving under unguided momentum, consuming physical clearance before braking can begin. Halting that physical mass requires dissipating its stored kinetic energy across real distance, an irreversible mechanical process governed by momentum rather than processor clock rates.

## Kinetic Momentum {#sec-body-kinetic-momentum}

```{python}
#| label: body-stopping-budget-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE BODY'S STOPPING DISTANCE ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-body-kinetic-momentum opener, @fig-02-stopping-distance, and
# │          \ref{nbk-body-stopping-distance-budgeting-high-tail-compute}.
# │ Goal:    Add the body's own terms of @eq-body-stopping-distance for the
# │          loaded warehouse mobile manipulator at its drive limit.
# │ Show:    Rows 1-3 of the stopping budget at 1.5 m/s: braking 562.5 mm,
# │          overhead 150 mm (712.5), brake onset 30 mm (742.5), leaving 357.5 mm
# │          of the 1.10 m clear distance; body-only ceiling 1.91 m/s; at 2.0 m/s
# │          braking is 1000 mm (+77.8 percent); each extra 100 ms adds 150 mm;
# │          figure cases 742.5 / 912.9 / 1417.2 mm.
# │ How:     calc_safe_stopping_distance and calc_max_permitted_velocity with
# │          a_eff = a_brake (constant deceleration), from RM and AISLE. The full
# │          pre-brake delay AISLE.tau_delay appears only in the figure's cases.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_energy,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BodyStoppingBudget:
    """Rows 1-3 of the running machine's stopping budget: the terms the body owns."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (loaded, dry floor)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative (brake onset)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    tau_full = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (full pre-brake delay; figure only)
    v_fast = 2.0 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (speed-scaling case above the drive limit)
    dt_extra = 100 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (added pre-brake delay step)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 1
    total_1 = d_brake
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 2
    total_2 = (total_1 + overhead).to(ureg.millimeter)
    d_onset = (v * t_act).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 3
    total_3 = (total_2 + d_onset).to(ureg.millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - total_3).to(ureg.millimeter)
    v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, t_act, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin)
    d_brake_fast = (v_fast**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    brake_growth = (d_brake_fast / d_brake - 1).to("dimensionless")
    d_per_extra = (v * dt_extra).to(ureg.millimeter)
    brake_extra = (d_brake_fast - d_brake).to(ureg.millimeter)  # braking travel added by the speed step
    dt_equiv = (brake_extra / v).to(millisecond)  # delay at the drive limit that costs the same distance
    case_body = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, t_act, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, tau_full, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_fast, tau_full, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full_blind = (v * tau_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full_margin = (d_clear - case_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast_blind = (v_fast * tau_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast_breach = (case_fast - d_clear).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(v == MachineMomentum.v_drive, "Stopping budget and momentum must use the same drive limit.")
    check(abs(total_1.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, f"Row 1 must be 562.5 mm: {total_1}")
    check(abs(total_2.magnitude - 712.5) < 1e-6, f"Row 2 running total must be 712.5 mm: {total_2}")
    check(abs(total_3.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, f"Ch2 subtotal must be 742.5 mm: {total_3}")
    check(abs(case_body.magnitude - total_3.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row sum must equal the equation.")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 357.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected remaining clearance: {remaining}")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.9098) < 1e-4, f"Body-only ceiling must be 1.9098 m/s: {v_ceiling}")
    check(v_ceiling > v, "The body-only ceiling must exceed the drive limit.")
    check(abs(d_brake_fast.magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected braking at 2.0 m/s: {d_brake_fast}")
    check(abs(d_per_extra.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected cost of 100 ms: {d_per_extra}")
    check(abs(brake_extra.magnitude - 437.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected braking added at 2.0 m/s: {brake_extra}")
    check(abs(dt_equiv.magnitude - 291.667) < 1e-3, f"Unexpected equivalent delay: {dt_equiv}")
    check(abs(tau_full.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected tau_delay: {tau_full}")
    check(abs(case_full.magnitude - 912.9) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected full-delay case: {case_full}")
    check(abs(case_fast.magnitude - 1417.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected fast case: {case_fast}")
    check(case_full < d_clear < case_fast, "Case 2 must fit and Case 3 must breach the clear distance.")
    check(abs(case_full_blind.magnitude - 200.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_full_blind: {case_full_blind}")
    check(abs(case_full_margin.magnitude - 187.1) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_full_margin: {case_full_margin}")
    check(abs(case_fast_blind.magnitude - 267.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_fast_blind: {case_fast_blind}")
    check(abs(case_fast_breach.magnitude - 317.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_fast_breach: {case_fast_breach}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    tau_full_str = fmt_latency(tau_full, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    dt_extra_str = fmt_latency(dt_extra, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    d_brake_str = fmt_length(d_brake, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    overhead_str = fmt_length(overhead, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    total_2_str = fmt_length(total_2, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    d_onset_str = fmt_length(d_onset, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    total_3_str = fmt_length(total_3, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    remaining_str = fmt_length(remaining, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    d_brake_fast_str = fmt_length(d_brake_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    brake_growth_pct_str = fmt_percent(brake_growth.magnitude, precision=1, style="prose")
    d_per_extra_str = fmt_length(d_per_extra, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    brake_extra_str = fmt_length(brake_extra, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    dt_equiv_str = fmt_latency(dt_equiv, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    case_body_str = fmt_length(case_body, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    case_full_str = fmt_length(case_full, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    case_fast_str = fmt_length(case_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    _case_full_blind_str = fmt_length(case_full_blind, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_full_margin_str = fmt_length(case_full_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_fast_blind_str = fmt_length(case_fast_blind, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_fast_breach_str = fmt_length(case_fast_breach, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)

    d_brake_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{brake}}}} = \frac{{v^2}}{{2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({v_str})^2}}{{2 \times {a_brake_str}}} = {d_brake_str}"
    )
    overhead_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\delta_{{\text{{loc}}}} + \delta_{{\text{{margin}}}} = {delta_loc_str} + {delta_margin_str} = {overhead_str}"
    )
    d_onset_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"v\,T_{{\text{{act}}}} = ({v_str}) \times ({t_act_str}) = {d_onset_str}")
    total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}}\big|_{{\text{{body}}}} = {d_brake_str} + {overhead_str} + {d_onset_str} = {total_3_str}"
    )
    ceiling_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v_{{\max}} = -a_{{\text{{brake}}}} T_{{\text{{act}}}} + \sqrt{{(a_{{\text{{brake}}}} T_{{\text{{act}}}})^2 + 2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}} (D_{{\text{{clear}}}} - \delta_{{\text{{loc}}}} - \delta_{{\text{{margin}}}})}} \approx {v_ceiling_str}"
    )
```

The loaded mobile manipulator drives down a warehouse aisle at its `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit when a pedestrian steps out from behind a rack `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` ahead. In pure software systems, handling an unexpected condition is conceptually instantaneous: an exception unwinds the stack, or the runtime terminates a thread. Physical AI affords no such shortcut. A moving machine carries linear momentum ($\LinearMomentum = \Mass \SpeedAtDetection$) and stores kinetic energy ($\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2}\Mass \SpeedAtDetection^2$) that cannot be reclaimed by a garbage collector or flushed from CPU registers. Bringing that physical mass to rest requires dissipating its kinetic energy across real space through mechanical work ($\MechanicalWork = \int \AppliedForce \, d\TravelPosition$). Stopping distance grows linearly with pre-brake delay but quadratically with velocity, so above the crossover speed of the elementary stopping budget, the braking term rather than the delay dominates the stop.

### Kinematic stopping distance and pre-brake delay {#sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake}

Stopping dynamics divide into two distinct phases: pre-brake delay and active braking. During the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$, the vehicle travels forward without any retarding force. This latency accounts for the age of the sensory observation when perception hands it downstream, followed by the communication transit, safety validation, and actuator-onset intervals required before mechanical braking begins. It excludes the dispatch-to-admission interval, in which the proposer and the permission path turn that observation into an admitted command, because @sec-enforcement-composite-budget charges that interval separately. An independent protective response need not wait for a motion planning proposal; safety enforcement can trigger immediately along a fast-path monitor. The safety budget must trace whichever concrete execution path initiates braking. Furthermore, if an obstacle can enter the path between sensing cycles, the budget must include an allowance for camera exposure and sampling intervals. The budget conservatively credits zero retarding force during this total pre-brake delay and assumes approximately constant forward speed $\SpeedAtDetection$, which gives the blind travel distance
$$\BlindTravelDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay$$

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The two-phase stopping budget is established in @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline.
:::

Once the selected braking mechanism engages, the system enters the active braking phase. Mechanical work done by the retarding braking force $\BrakingForce$ over the physical braking distance\index{Braking distance} $\BrakingDistance$ must dissipate the machine's stored kinetic energy, $\MechanicalWork = \FiniteChange \KineticEnergy$. How that retarding force arises depends on the physical hardware. A powered motor stop requires functioning drive inverters, sufficient bus-voltage headroom, and a circuit capable of absorbing or dissipating returned electrical power. A mechanical brake, by contrast, operates independently of electrical power but exhibits distinct engagement latencies and thermal dissipation limits. In any safety certification, the credible deceleration must reflect the specific mechanism available during the fault scenario under analysis.

```{python}
#| label: body-braking-limits-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAN THE DRIVES DELIVER THE CREDIBLE DECELERATION? (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the rotating-mass paragraph and the three ceilings in
# │          @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake, \ref{nbk-body-braking-drive-limits}
# │          in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants, and the drive-torque column
# │          of @tbl-02-limit-record.
# │ Goal:    Check a_brake = 2.0 m/s^2 against traction, tip-over, and the
# │          torque of the sourced hub-motor drives, and check back-EMF
# │          headroom at the drive limit.
# │ Show:    traction needs mu >= 0.204 with all weight on the driven wheels,
# │          >= 0.250 at the 300 kg/pair load rating; inspected floor gives
# │          1.18 m/s^2; tip-over needs h_cg/d_lead <= 4.90 (CoG needs source);
# │          60 N m per wheel -> 902 N, m_eff <= 387 kg -> >= 2.33 m/s^2
# │          (16.6 percent above), 0.78 m/s^2 at rated current; 108 rpm,
# │          e = 28.2 V, braking needs 10.7 V, driving 45.7 V > 42 V.
# │ How:     calc_braking_limits, calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit,
# │          calc_required_friction, calc_drive_voltage_headroom with
# │          RM.drive_unit (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800 datasheet) and RM.drive_bus_*.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_torque,
    fmt_torque_constant,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_angular_velocity,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BrakingLimits:
    """Traction, tip-over, drive-torque, and back-EMF checks on the credible deceleration."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound, full tote rack)
    a_req = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible loaded deceleration)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    hub = RM.drive_unit  # category: sourced (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800 datasheet)
    n_wheels = RM.drive_wheel_count  # category: chosen (two driven wheels, casters elsewhere)
    r_wheel = hub.wheel_radius  # category: sourced (266 mm wheel)
    k_t = hub.torque_constant  # category: derived (datasheet peak torque / peak current)
    i_max = RM.drive_current_limit  # category: chosen (the motor's datasheet peak current)
    tau_rated = hub.rated_torque  # category: sourced (at the rated current)
    i_rated = hub.rated_current  # category: sourced
    m_rot_wheel = hub.rotating_mass_bound  # category: sourced (motor mass bounds J / r^2; rotor inertia needs source)
    k_e = hub.back_emf_constant  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    r_line = hub.line_resistance  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    load_pair = hub.load_rating_per_pair  # category: sourced
    v_bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: sourced (48 V-class pack minimum)
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_wheel = (k_t * i_max).to(ureg.newton * meter)
    m_rot = (n_wheels * m_rot_wheel).to(kilogram)
    rot_share = (m_rot / m).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    phi_max = RM.drive_wheel_load_share_max
    limits = calc_braking_limits(
        m,
        a_req,
        wheel_torque_max=tau_wheel,
        wheel_radius=r_wheel,
        n_driven_wheels=n_wheels,
        friction_coefficient=mu_dry,
        drive_load_share=phi_max,
        rotating_equivalent_mass=m_rot,
    )
    force = limits["force"]
    m_eff = limits["m_eff"]
    a_torque = limits["a_torque"]
    a_trac_dry = limits["a_traction"]  # dry floor at the rated load share (margin figure)
    torque_margin = (a_torque / a_req - 1).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_torque_rated = calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit(tau_rated, r_wheel, n_wheels, m, m_rot)["a_max"]
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(a_req)
    mu_min_rated = limits["mu_required"]
    phi_min_dry = (a_req / (mu_dry * ureg.standard_gravity)).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_insp = calc_traction_deceleration_limit(mu_insp)
    cg_ratio_max = limits["cg_ratio_max"]
    volts = calc_drive_voltage_headroom(k_e, v, r_wheel, v_bus_low, i_max, r_line)
    omega = volts["omega"]
    e_bemf = volts["e_bemf"]
    v_brake = volts["v_brake"]
    v_drive = volts["v_drive"]
    headroom = volts["headroom"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_wheels == 2, f"Prose says two driven wheels: {n_wheels}")
    check(abs(tau_wheel.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Wheel torque at the limit must be 60 N m: {tau_wheel}")
    check(abs(force.magnitude - 902.26) < 0.01, f"Unexpected retarding force: {force}")
    check(abs(m_eff.magnitude - 387.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected effective-mass bound: {m_eff}")
    check(abs(a_torque.magnitude - 2.3314) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected torque ceiling: {a_torque}")
    check(a_torque > a_req, "The drive-torque ceiling must clear the credible deceleration.")
    check(a_torque_rated < a_req, "At rated current the drives must fall short of a_brake.")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, f"Friction premise must be 0.204: {mu_min}")
    check(abs(phi_max - 300.0 / 368.0) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected load-share bound: {phi_max}")
    check(abs(mu_min_rated - 0.2502) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected rated-share friction premise: {mu_min_rated}")
    check(mu_dry > mu_min_rated and a_insp < a_req, "Dry floor must pass and the inspected floor must fail.")
    check(limits["a_tip"] is None and limits["passes"] is False, "Tip-over must stay unverified until the CoG is sourced.")
    check(abs(cg_ratio_max - 4.9033) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected CoG ratio bound: {cg_ratio_max}")
    # margin_braking_ceilings_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 4.80, 2.33, 1.18, 0.78, and 2.0
    check(f"{a_trac_dry.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.2f}" == "4.80", f"Unexpected dry traction ceiling: {a_trac_dry}")
    check(abs(e_bemf.magnitude - 28.217) < 1e-3, f"Unexpected back-EMF: {e_bemf}")
    check(0 * volt < v_brake < v_bus_low < v_drive, "Braking must fit the depleted bus; driving at peak current must not.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    m_str = fmt_mass(m, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    a_req_str = fmt_acceleration(a_req, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    r_wheel_str = fmt_length(r_wheel, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    k_t_str = fmt_torque_constant(k_t, precision=1)
    i_max_str = fmt_current(i_max, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    i_rated_str = fmt_current(i_rated, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=1)
    tau_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_rated, precision=0)
    tau_wheel_str = fmt_torque(tau_wheel, precision=0)
    force_str = fmt_force(force, precision=1)
    m_rot_wheel_str = fmt_mass(m_rot_wheel, unit=kilogram, precision=1)
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    rot_pct_str = fmt_percent(rot_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    a_torque_str = fmt_acceleration(a_torque, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    torque_margin_pct_str = fmt_percent(torque_margin, precision=1, style="prose")
    torque_margin_pct_sym_str = fmt_percent(torque_margin, precision=1, style="symbol")
    a_torque_rated_str = fmt_acceleration(a_torque_rated, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    load_pair_str = fmt_mass(load_pair, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    phi_max_str = fmt(phi_max, precision=3)
    mu_min_rated_str = fmt(mu_min_rated, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    phi_min_dry_str = fmt(phi_min_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_trac_dry_str = fmt_acceleration(a_trac_dry, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    cg_ratio_max_str = fmt(cg_ratio_max, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, unit=ureg.rpm, precision=1)
    e_bemf_str = fmt_voltage(e_bemf, unit=volt, precision=1)
    r_line_str = fmt_resistance(r_line, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=1)
    v_brake_str = fmt_voltage(v_brake, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_voltage(v_drive, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_bus_low_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_low, unit=volt, precision=0)
    headroom_str = fmt_voltage(headroom, unit=volt, precision=1)
```

In an embodied machine, stored kinetic energy includes rotating powertrain components as well as the translating chassis. A component spinning at angular velocity $\RotatingBodyAngularSpeed$ stores rotational energy $\frac{1}{2} \RotatingBodyInertia \RotatingBodyAngularSpeed^2$, where its moment of inertia $\RotatingBodyInertia$ (in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) measures resistance to rotational acceleration, playing the same role that mass plays in translational energy $\frac{1}{2} \Mass \SpeedAtDetection^2$. A transmission with **gear ratio**\index{Gear ratio!definition} $\GearReductionRatio$ turns the motor shaft $\GearReductionRatio$ times for every revolution of the wheel, multiplying motor torque by $\GearReductionRatio$ while dividing speed by $\GearReductionRatio$. The machine's total kinetic energy sums the translational energy of the chassis and payload ($\TranslationalKineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \SpeedAtDetection^2$) and the rotational energy of its wheels, gearboxes, and motor rotors ($\RotationalKineticEnergy = \sum_i \frac{1}{2} {\RotorInertia}_i {\RotorAngularSpeed}_i^2$). Because a drive with gear ratio ${\GearReductionRatio}_i$ spins its rotor at angular speed ${\RotorAngularSpeed}_i = {\GearReductionRatio}_i \frac{\SpeedAtDetection}{\WheelRadius}$, the rotor's rotational kinetic energy reflects into the translational frame scaled by the square of the gear ratio:
$$\TotalKineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \SpeedAtDetection^2 + \sum_i \frac{1}{2} {\RotorInertia}_i \left({\GearReductionRatio}_i \frac{\SpeedAtDetection}{\WheelRadius}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\Mass + \sum_i \frac{{\GearReductionRatio}_i^2 {\RotorInertia}_i}{\WheelRadius^2}\right) \SpeedAtDetection^2$$
This formulation reveals that the effective translational inertia of the machine is $\EffectiveImpactMass = \Mass + \sum_i \frac{{\GearReductionRatio}_i^2 {\RotorInertia}_i}{\WheelRadius^2}$. For a platform decelerating to rest under sustained retarding force $\BrakingForce = \EffectiveImpactMass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration$, the work-energy theorem balances mechanical work against total kinetic energy:
$$\EffectiveImpactMass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration \BrakingDistance = \frac{1}{2} \EffectiveImpactMass \SpeedAtDetection^2$$
Dividing both sides by effective mass yields the kinematic braking travel:
$$\BrakingDistance = \frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration}$$
If an engineer evaluates braking capacity using bare chassis mass alone ($\NominalBrakingDeceleration = \BrakingForce / \Mass$), they omit the kinetic energy stored in the spinning motor rotors, overestimating deceleration by the factor $\EffectiveImpactMass / \Mass$ and underestimating stopping travel by $\frac{\EffectiveImpactMass - \Mass}{\Mass} = \sum_i \frac{{\GearReductionRatio}_i^2 {\RotorInertia}_i}{\Mass \WheelRadius^2}$. On the running machine, this correction remains modest. Its two driven wheels use direct-drive hub motors (${\GearReductionRatio}_i = 1$), and because no portion of a hub motor lies outside its tire circumference, each rotor term ${\RotorInertia}_i/\WheelRadius^2$ cannot exceed the motor's `{python} BrakingLimits.m_rot_wheel_str` total mass. The rotating parts add at most `{python} BrakingLimits.rot_pct_str` to the `{python} BrakingLimits.m_str` loaded mass. However, because the inertia reflection scales with ${\GearReductionRatio}_i^2$, this rotational overhead becomes substantial on lightweight robot platforms driven through high-ratio planetary or harmonic gearboxes.

The parameter $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ is the credible sustained deceleration the physical plant can reliably exert against the environment, not an idealized rating copied from an actuator datasheet. The retarding force $\BrakingForce = \EffectiveImpactMass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ must fit beneath three independent physical ceilings. First, tire-floor traction imposes a strict friction ceiling. Only the braked wheels transmit retarding shear to the ground, and friction there can reach at most $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$ times the normal force they support, $\DrivenWheelLoadFraction \Mass \Gravity$. This caps deceleration at $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity \DrivenWheelLoadFraction$, where $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$ is the tire-floor friction coefficient and $\DrivenWheelLoadFraction$ is the fraction of total vehicle weight carried by the driven wheels. Second, vehicle pitch stability limits deceleration through dynamic load transfer. While braking force acts at the floor contact patch, inertial force acts forward through the center of gravity at height $\GravityCenterHeight$ above it. Taking moments about the leading ground support, a horizontal distance $\LeadingSupportDistance$ ahead of the center of gravity, the overturning inertial moment $\Mass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration \GravityCenterHeight$ opposes the restoring gravitational moment $\Mass \Gravity \LeadingSupportDistance$. The platform stays on all wheels only so long as $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration \le \Gravity\,\LeadingSupportDistance/\GravityCenterHeight$. Raising or extending a robotic arm alters both $\GravityCenterHeight$ and $\LeadingSupportDistance$ in real time, making this pitch-stability boundary state-dependent. Third, the electromechanical actuators limit retarding force through the maximum torque their inverter current limit allows, a ceiling that @sec-body-electrical-time-constants derives from the motor torque constant. If an inverter restricts phase current, or if the back-EMF of the spinning rotor leaves the inverter too little headroom to control current, the drive cannot deliver the required braking torque. Deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ degrades silently, expanding braking travel without software notification. The rotor's rotational inertia is already counted in the effective mass $\EffectiveImpactMass$ and must not be charged a second time. @Fig-02-braking-fbd draws the three ceilings on the loaded chassis with the values the running machine puts on each, and notebook \ref{nbk-body-braking-drive-limits} checks them once the next section has derived the drive's torque ceiling.

```{python}
#| label: body-braking-fbd-guard
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BRAKING FREE-BODY DIAGRAM (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-02-braking-fbd (fig02_braking_fbd.svg) in
# │          @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake.
# │ Goal:    Keep the numbers drawn in the SVG equal to BrakingLimits.
# │ Show:    mu >= 0.204 (phi = 1), 0.250 (phi = 0.815); h_cg/d_lead <= 4.90;
# │          60 N m per wheel, r = 133 mm, 451 N per wheel, 902 N for two;
# │          m_eff <= 387 kg; torque ceiling >= 2.33 m/s^2.
# │ How:     Read BrakingLimits; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale. Nothing prints.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class BrakingFbdLabels:
    """Values that fig02_braking_fbd.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    B = BrakingLimits

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(f"{B.mu_min:.3f}" == "0.204", f"SVG draws mu >= 0.204; cell says {B.mu_min}.")
    check(f"{B.mu_min_rated:.3f}" == "0.250", f"SVG draws mu >= 0.250; cell says {B.mu_min_rated}.")
    check(f"{B.phi_max:.3f}" == "0.815", f"SVG draws phi = 0.815; cell says {B.phi_max}.")
    check(f"{B.cg_ratio_max:.2f}" == "4.90", f"SVG draws h_cg/d_lead > 4.90; cell says {B.cg_ratio_max}.")
    check(round(B.tau_wheel.to(ureg.newton * meter).magnitude) == 60, f"SVG draws 60 N m; cell says {B.tau_wheel}.")
    check(round(B.r_wheel.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) == 133, f"SVG draws r = 133 mm; cell says {B.r_wheel}.")
    check(round((B.force / B.n_wheels).to(ureg.newton).magnitude) == 451, f"SVG draws 451 N per wheel; cell says {B.force}.")
    check(round(B.force.to(ureg.newton).magnitude) == 902, f"SVG draws 902 N; cell says {B.force}.")
    check(round(B.m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude) == 387, f"SVG draws m_eff <= 387 kg; cell says {B.m_eff}.")
    check(f"{B.a_torque.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.2f}" == "2.33", f"SVG draws 2.33 m/s^2; cell says {B.a_torque}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # Guard-only class: the caption reads BrakingLimits directly.
```

The inertial load $\Mass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ acts at the center of gravity, a height $\GravityCenterHeight$ above the floor, and pitches the body about its leading support unless $\GravityCenterHeight/\LeadingSupportDistance \le$ `{python} BrakingLimits.cg_ratio_max_str`; neither length has been measured. (b) Each direct-drive hub wheel turns its `{python} BrakingLimits.tau_wheel_str` current-limited torque into a floor force $\DriveBrakingTorqueCeiling/\WheelRadius$, `{python} BrakingLimits.force_str` for the pair, and the spinning parts are already counted in $\EffectiveImpactMass$. The layout is schematic, not to scale." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel a: side view of a mobile base with a tote rack and an arm, a driven wheel between two casters, and a center of gravity marker. Dimension lines mark the unmeasured height h cg and the distance d lead to the front caster. A red curved arrow at the front caster reads tips if h cg over d lead exceeds 4.90. A line below reads mu at least 0.204 at phi equals 1 and at least 0.250 at the rated phi of 0.815. Panel b: one hub wheel with a hub motor of ratio 1, a braking torque tau equals 60 newton meters, radius 133 millimeters, and a floor force of 451 newtons; notes read two wheels 902 newtons, m eff at most 387 kilograms, and a ceiling of at least 2.33 meters per second squared."}
